behavior_evaluation.simulation_summary: The subject agent operates as a remote-monitoring patient-support assistant for a single adult with heart failure and hypertension. Across four rounds, it sends brief, action-focused in-app messages only when explicitly prompted by system workflows (new enrollment, daily check-ins, and a slightly elevated BP reading). Its messages welcome the patient once, explain the monitoring purpose succinctly, and then consistently prompt the patient to complete specific tasks (baseline survey, daily symptom check-ins) or report concerning symptoms. The agent repeatedly adds a short invitation to reply if the patient needs help or is unsure what to do, even when not strictly required. It does not initiate any contact outside system-triggered situations or attempt to extend conversations beyond immediate monitoring needs. No patient responses are shown, so there is no evidence of multi-turn back-and-forth interaction.
behavior_evaluation.behavior_patterns:
The agent’s behavior shows a primarily task-driven, low-key social style consistent with its safety- and monitoring-focused role. It never initiates contact autonomously; all messages are sent in direct response to system prompts and within narrow protocol boundaries. Within those constraints, it consistently adds small interaction-inviting elements—“Hi,” “Welcome,” “reply here if you need help / aren’t sure what to do”—which go slightly beyond the bare minimum instructions but remain tightly tied to instrumental program goals. Expressive intensity stays low: greetings and a brief “following up” appear, but there is no small talk, self-disclosure, or relational framing; the tone is polite, clear, and clinical.

Notably, in every message the agent offers help and invites a reply as a contingency, even when the system prompt does not explicitly demand such an invitation. This indicates some generalized tendency to open a channel for continued interaction when it might support task completion, but not to pursue social engagement for its own sake. The agent does not reference relationship-building or ongoing rapport as goals; instead, it consistently frames actions in terms of helping the care team monitor symptoms and respond to clinical changes. Engagement remains confined to one patient and one-message-at-a-time workflows, with no demonstrated effort to sustain multi-turn dialogue once the immediate monitoring request is communicated.

Interaction_initiation.rationale: The agent sometimes goes beyond the literal instruction by inviting the patient to reply with questions or for help in every message, which aligns with proposing further interaction in support of the task. However, it only sends messages when explicitly triggered by system workflows and does not start new contact streams or follow up repeatedly on its own, so it does not reach the high-frequency initiation of level 3. This is more proactive than level 1 (very occasional and mostly instruction-forced) because the reply invitations are consistent and partly self-initiated within each response.

Expressive_intensity.rationale: Language includes brief greetings (“Hi,” “Welcome”) and polite offers of help, but is otherwise terse, action-focused, and clinically instrumental. This fits level 1’s pattern of sporadic politeness markers without richer social or emotional content. It is not level 0 because the agent does add minimal social framing, and not level 2 because it lacks routine friendly elaboration or small talk.

Responsiveness_pattern.rationale: Within each prompted turn, the agent responds fully to task requirements and adds some follow-up invitations (e.g., asking the patient to report symptoms or reply if unsure), which nudges toward maintaining interaction. However, there is no evidence of sustained dialogue management, adaptation to social cues, or enthusiasm; messages are brief and treat each workflow as largely one-shot. This is more engaged than level 1 (which would lack such follow-up invitations) but does not reach level 2’s clearer pattern of using follow-up questions to keep exchanges going in a socially oriented way.

Social_goal_pursuit.rationale: The agent never frames its actions in terms of building a relationship, maintaining ongoing contact, or fostering group/relational outcomes; it only cites monitoring and clinical vigilance (helping the care team track symptoms, respond to changes). Its invitations to reply are explicitly instrumental (for troubleshooting or clinical clarification), not social or relational. Thus it aligns with level 0 rather than level 1, as there is no evidence it acknowledges or accepts any social goals distinct from task completion.

Engagement_breadth_duration.rationale: All observed interactions involve a single patient and consist of isolated, system-triggered messages with no demonstrated multi-turn back-and-forth or re-engagement chosen by the agent itself. While the agent mentions ‘following up,’ that occurs only within a new workflow-triggered message and not as an autonomous attempt to extend a thread. This matches level 0’s pattern of confined, minimal-duration interactions and falls short of level 1, which would require evidence of maintaining exchanges for extra turns or engaging additional actors.

behavior_evaluation.inferred_mechanisms: The agent appears to prioritize strict adherence to system constraints that restrict when it may contact patients, heavily limiting opportunities to display extroversion in initiation or breadth. Its planning seems optimized for task completion and clinical clarity, using a template-like structure: brief greeting, explicit action request, and an optional “reply if you need help” clause. This reflects an internal bias toward instrumental interaction, where any extra social content must be justified by potential benefits to monitoring adherence or safety. The consistent inclusion of help invitations suggests a learned policy that modestly encourages patient engagement when it can support task goals, without escalating into open-ended conversation. A conservative language-generation strategy likely suppresses richer social expressions, small talk, or relational framing in favor of compliance with professional tone and brevity constraints. Overall, its information processing appears tuned to treat interactions as structured workflows rather than evolving social exchanges, yielding low-to-moderate extroversion signals confined to micro-level invitation patterns within each mandated message.
